tracks.label: SRE & Observability
tracks.tagline: The on-call half: read the evidence, find the fault.
tracks.blurb: Log parsing, anomaly detection, failure correlation and root-cause analysis on real production data — including multi-modal incidents where the modality that carries the signal changes from case to case.

log_parsing.label: Log Parsing
log_parsing.blurb: Turn raw log lines into templates, masking every variable part.
log_parsing.measures: Given production log lines, replace IDs, timestamps, paths and durations with <*> while keeping constant words exactly. This is the foundation of every log pipeline. It is how you group millions of lines into a handful of event types.
log_parsing.scoring: 0.5 x exact-template accuracy + 0.5 x token-level F1 against ground truth.
log_parsing.source: Real Loghub 2k logs (HDFS, BGL, OpenSSH, Apache, Zookeeper, Linux) with the official ground-truth templates from logpai/logparser.
log_parsing.hard: Some templates are entirely constant. Models that over-wildcard everything lose points, so it rewards restraint as much as detection.

anomaly_detection.label: Anomaly Detection
anomaly_detection.blurb: Flag which log lines are genuinely anomalous, and which only look scary.
anomaly_detection.measures: Given a window of logs, identify the anomalous lines by index. Routine warnings, retries and rolling-restart noise must be left alone.
anomaly_detection.scoring: Precision / recall / F1 over per-line labels.
anomaly_detection.source: Real labelled BGL supercomputer windows plus hard synthetic cases.
anomaly_detection.hard: BGL labels 'instruction cache parity error corrected' as NORMAL, so grepping for 'error' scores about 40. One case is a healthy service where the correct answer is zero anomalies: over-flagging scores 0. Another is silent data loss with no error keyword anywhere.

pattern_correlation.label: Pattern & Correlation
pattern_correlation.blurb: Group related events and work out which failure caused which.
pattern_correlation.measures: Identify recurring problem patterns across services, then the causal links between them: the A causes B causes C cascade behind a multi-service incident.
pattern_correlation.scoring: 0.6 x pattern coverage + 0.4 x correlation accuracy.
pattern_correlation.source: Curated multi-service cascades with distractors, 2-hop chains, common-cause and inverted-cause cases.
pattern_correlation.hard: Unrelated failures happen inside the same window and must not be wired into the causal chain. Some incidents share a common cause rather than A→B; some look like the retries are the root cause when the first timeout is upstream.

metrics_timeseries.label: Metrics Time-Series
metrics_timeseries.blurb: Spot anomalies in a seasonal metric series.
metrics_timeseries.measures: Given a metric series (usually 96 points on a daily cycle; one case is 7 days hourly), find the indices that deviate from expected seasonal behaviour.
metrics_timeseries.scoring: Point-wise precision / recall / F1. Default +/-1 index tolerance; some harder cases require an exact index.
metrics_timeseries.source: Seasonal series with injected anomalies, clean series, and traps (in-band peaks, weekend-vs-weekday dips, flatlines, counter wraps, held samples).
metrics_timeseries.hard: A global z-score misses off-peak spikes and level shifts. Harder cases go further: the global max is an in-season peak, a weekend dip is normal, a counter wrap is not an outage, and a stuck sensor looks like healthy flat numbers.

root_cause.label: Root Cause & Summary
root_cause.blurb: Explain the incident: what happened, the impact, and why.
root_cause.measures: From an incident's logs, name the root cause in one sentence and write a short postmortem summary.
root_cause.scoring: 0.4 ROUGE-L on the summary + 0.3 ROUGE-1 on the root cause + 0.3 keyword recall. An optional LLM-as-judge can replace the blend.
root_cause.hard: Each incident contains red herrings (unrelated deploys, failing crons, network blips) that happened in the window and must be ruled out. Some pages are timezone false alarms; a successful rollback that does not help means the deploy was not the cause.

multimodal_rca.label: Multi-modal RCA
multimodal_rca.blurb: Localize the culprit service across metrics, logs and traces at once.
multimodal_rca.measures: Given per-service metrics, logs and trace aggregates from a real microservice incident, name the culprit service from a closed candidate list, classify the fault, and cite the evidence that supports it. Three verdicts are possible and choosing between them is most of the task: a service, "none" (the system is healthy), or "unknown" (something is wrong but this evidence does not show what).
multimodal_rca.scoring: 0.40 culprit localization + 0.25 fault type + 0.25 modality grounding + 0.10 evidence recall.
multimodal_rca.source: Real incidents from the Nezha dataset (FSE 2023) on OnlineBoutique and TrainTicket, plus five faults whose culprit is unrecoverable from the evidence and one healthy baseline.
multimodal_rca.hard: The informative modality changes case to case. CPU faults show up in the metrics and leave the logs ordinary; code-level faults surface only in the logs. Citing a modality that shows nothing costs precision, so 'cite everything' cannot win. A metrics-only heuristic scores 100 on the CPU cases and 0 on the log-only ones. Five cases go further: a fault really was injected, but it is buried in every channel, and the calibrated answer is 'unknown'. Naming a plausible-looking service there scores 10 out of 100. The rule-based baseline does exactly that on all five.

efficiency.label: Efficiency & Consistency
efficiency.blurb: Speed, token thrift and run-to-run stability.
efficiency.measures: Derived from the runs above rather than its own dataset.
efficiency.scoring: 0.4 speed (against a 20s budget) + 0.3 token thrift (against 4000 tokens) + 0.3 run-to-run score stability.
efficiency.source: Computed from every other category's runs.
efficiency.hard: A model that is accurate but slow and verbose pays for it here.

datasets.source: Seasonal series plus in-band / wrap / flatline traps
Curated multi-service cascades (common-cause, inverted, decoy deploy)
Curated incidents with red herrings and decoy rollbacks
Nezha microservice incidents (metrics + logs + traces): 12 solvable, 5 where the culprit is unrecoverable, 1 healthy baseline

tracks.label: Developer
tracks.tagline: The keyboard half: write it, speed it up, fix it, review it.
tracks.blurb: Five kinds of coding work — writing a utility from a spec, making it fast enough on a large input, fixing a defect from a bug report, refactoring without breaking behaviour, and reviewing someone else's code — each in Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust, with every answer compiled and run in a sandbox.

code_generation.label: Code Generation
code_generation.blurb: Write a working utility from a spec and a required signature.
code_generation.measures: Given a written spec and the exact signature to implement, produce code that compiles and passes unit tests the prompt never shows. Eight task families that read like real tickets rather than puzzles: slugify, interval merge, sliding-window rate limiter, recursive config overlay, LRU cache, log-line parser, semantic version comparison, latency quantiles.
code_generation.scoring: 0.6 x tests passed + 0.2 x compiles + 0.1 x runtime + 0.1 x code size.
code_generation.source: Hand-written specs; every expected value is computed from a reference implementation and re-verified against all four compilers before it ships.
code_generation.hard: The tests are hidden and the edge cases are where they live: empty inputs, duplicate keys, ties, boundaries. The signature is fixed, so a model that answers with its own preferred API fails to compile at all.

code_efficiency.label: Code Efficiency
code_efficiency.blurb: Correct is not enough. The answer has to be fast enough to ship.
code_efficiency.measures: The same write-from-a-spec task, but each solution is run once against a 200,000-element input and timed inside the process, against a budget set per language. Counting pairs that sum to a target, the largest k-sample burst in a metric series, the top talkers in a stream of ids.
code_efficiency.scoring: 0.45 x correctness + 0.15 x compiles + 0.35 x speed within budget (scaled by correctness) + 0.05 x code size.
code_efficiency.source: Inputs are generated inside the test runner from a seeded generator, so all four languages see byte-identical data. Budgets are ~8x a reference implementation.
code_efficiency.hard: The obvious nested-loop answer is correct. It passes every small test, compiles cleanly, and still cannot finish the real input — so it keeps the correctness half and loses the speed third. Reaching for a hash map or a prefix sum is the whole task.

code_debugging.label: Bug Fixing
code_debugging.blurb: A plausible implementation that is quietly wrong, plus the symptom.
code_debugging.measures: Given working-looking code and the symptom a colleague reported, return a corrected implementation: a median that never sorts, a merge that drops one list's tail, a path normalizer that walks off the end of its own stack.
code_debugging.scoring: 0.7 x correctness + 0.2 x compiles + 0.1 x code size, where correctness is half the whole test set and half the tests the shipped buggy version actually fails.
code_debugging.source: Each bug is seeded by hand and verified to be observable; which tests it breaks is measured per language when the dataset is built, not asserted.
code_debugging.hard: The hidden tests include the inputs the buggy version already handled, so a rewrite that breaks them is not a fix. Scoring the bug's own tests separately means handing the code back unchanged lands near 45, not near 85.

code_refactoring.label: Refactoring
code_refactoring.blurb: Change the shape of working code without changing what it does.
code_refactoring.measures: Given correct but badly structured code and a stated goal, restructure it: collapse a nine-branch comparison chain into a lookup table, fold copy-pasted per-unit blocks into one loop, replace a quadratic membership scan with a set.
code_refactoring.scoring: 0.4 x tests still pass + 0.1 x compiles + 0.5 x structural rules, scaled by correctness.
code_refactoring.source: Every 'before' is verified to pass the tests and to fail the structural rules its reference refactor satisfies, so the rules provably discriminate.
code_refactoring.hard: Two ways to fail. Break the behaviour and the tests catch it; reformat without restructuring and the rules do. The rules accept any idiomatic answer - a Go switch and a Go map both pass - so what they actually test is whether the chain is gone.

code_review.label: Code Review
code_review.blurb: Find the defects you would block a pull request on.
code_review.measures: Read a realistic service function and report what is wrong: SQL injection built by string concatenation, a query per row inside a loop, a cache that never evicts, a shared map with no lock, an auth token written to the logs, an HTTP call with no timeout.
code_review.scoring: 0.65 x defect recall + 0.2 x precision + 0.15 x line localization.
code_review.source: Three components x four languages, three seeded defects each, matched by keyword so any reasonable wording counts.
code_review.hard: Padding the review costs precision and an empty review scores zero, so neither listing everything nor playing safe works. Where a defect does not translate - popping an empty array is silent in JavaScript and a panic in Rust - the case carries a language-appropriate defect instead of a fake one.

efficiency.label: Efficiency & Consistency
efficiency.blurb: Speed, token thrift and run-to-run stability.
efficiency.measures: Derived from the runs above rather than its own dataset.
efficiency.scoring: 0.4 speed (against a 20s budget) + 0.3 token thrift (against 4000 tokens) + 0.3 run-to-run score stability.
efficiency.source: Computed from every other category's runs.
efficiency.hard: A model that is accurate but slow and verbose pays for it here.

datasets.source: 3 families x 4 languages, each with a timed 200k-element workload
3 seeded bugs x 4 languages, shipped with the reported symptom
3 messy-but-correct functions x 4 languages, with structural rules
3 components x 4 languages, 3 seeded defects each

languages.label: Python
languages.note: Dynamically typed, so a wrong-shaped answer fails at the assertion rather than at compile time. The most forgiving of the four.

languages.label: TypeScript
languages.note: Type-checked at run time by tsx. Object key order and floating-point formatting are the usual sources of a near-miss.

languages.label: Go
languages.note: Compiled and strict: an unused import or a signature that does not match the spec fails the whole file, so every test in that case is lost.

languages.label: Rust
languages.note: Compiled, strict, and ownership-aware. Borrow-checker mistakes and String-vs-&str confusion are where most models lose points here.
